title: Netanyahu's Likud Holds High-Stakes Primaries: Only 15 Spots Actually Up for Grabs
summary:
Imagine a race where almost half the starting lineup is already decided before the starting gun fires. That's the reality of Monday's Likud party primaries in Israel, where Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing party is selecting its candidate list for a general election that could reshape the country's political landscape.

Under Israel's proportional representation system, voters choose a party, and seats in the 120-member Knesset are allocated based on each party's share of the vote. In the last election, Likud won 23.4 percent, which translated into 32 seats—meaning the top 32 names on the party's list became lawmakers. This year, however, the competition is unusually constrained.

Netanyahu, as party leader, is granted eight personal picks on the list. Additionally, three other sitting Knesset members—Foreign Minister Gideon Saar, Defense Minister Israel Katz, and Likud Constitution Committee Chair Haim Katz—have secured uncontested spots through merger deals and special arrangements. That means out of the top 30 realistic positions, only 15 are genuinely open in the primaries. The rest are already locked in.

Those guaranteed spots carry significant weight. Defense Minister Israel Katz is one of the most hardline voices in the government. In October 2023, he publicly called for cutting water, electricity, and fuel supplies to Gaza and withholding humanitarian aid until Israeli hostages were returned. More recently, he has backed maintaining an Israeli security zone around Gaza and announced plans for new Israeli settlements in the enclave. Foreign Minister Gideon Saar has taken similarly uncompromising positions on the war and on Israel's international critics.

The primaries themselves are known for being raucous and contentious—a reflection of the broader political stakes. Likud has dominated Israeli politics for decades, credited with shifting the country's center of gravity dramatically to the right. Under Netanyahu's leadership, the party has overseen major military campaigns and actively worked against the two-state solution.

With a general election looming, the outcome of these primaries will help determine not just who sits in the Knesset, but the direction of Israeli policy on war, peace, and the future of Gaza. For the candidates fighting for those 15 open spots, the battle is fierce—and for the country, the consequences could be profound.
why_it_matters: Who fills Likud's guaranteed and contestable spots can determine whether Israeli policy continues toward harder-line security measures, settlement expansion, or renewed diplomacy—a choice that affects regional stability and the lives of people in the same region as young readers.

background_read: Israel's Knesset is a 120-member parliament elected through proportional representation, meaning parties submit ranked lists and voters choose a party rather than individual local candidates.

Likud, a right-wing party led by Benjamin Netanyahu (Israel's longest-serving prime minister), has dominated Israeli politics for decades and is widely credited with shifting the country's political centre of gravity rightward.
Gideon Saar (foreign minister) and Israel Katz (defense minister) are senior security cabinet figures known for hardline positions on the war in Gaza and on Israel's international critics.
The two-state solution—an independent Palestinian state alongside Israel—has long been the main international framework for peace, but Israel's current government rejects it.
Gaza, a narrow coastal territory along the Mediterranean Sea, has been the focus of a major war since the October 7, 2023 attack and remains central to Israel's security debate.

perspectives.perspective: Likud party loyalists and Netanyahu supporters
perspectives.description: They see the primaries as an internal party process that rewards loyalty and ensures strong national-security voices enter the Knesset. To them, guaranteed spots for experienced leaders provide continuity during a war and prevent dangerous political experiments.

They view the guaranteed spots as a sign that the party is entrenching hardline policies—control of Gaza, settlement expansion, and rejection of Palestinian statehood. In this view, the primaries narrow the path to a negotiated two-state solution and deepen Palestinian suffering.

Analysts focus on electoral mechanics: under proportional representation and internal party rules, most top list slots are effectively decided before ordinary members vote. They note that the competition is real but far smaller than it appears, which raises questions about intraparty democracy.

They argue the primary results may signal how far Israel goes toward annexation, security zones, or renewed ceasefire diplomacy after the upcoming election. If hardline candidates win the open slots, external mediators and neighboring states may face an even tougher diplomatic landscape.
